summary: This standards-track RFC describes how a JSON Web Token can declare that its presenter holds a particular proof-of-possession key, and how the recipient can confirm that cryptographically. This helps prevent a stolen token from being used by someone else.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7800 lets a JSON Web Token say which key its holder must be able to use. The token carries that key in a 'cnf' claim, and the party receiving the token checks that the sender can prove it holds the key. A copied token is then not enough on its own to get past the check.

subtitle: How a JSON Web Token can name a key that only its holder can use, so a stolen token is not enough.

tldr.problem: A JSON Web Token proves who issued it, but on its own it does not stop anyone who steals it from using it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a 'cnf' confirmation claim to the JWT whose members name a proof-of-possession key, either by value ('jwk', 'jwe') or by reference ('kid', 'jku'), so the recipient can check that the presenter holds that key.
tldr.outcome: A recipient can now reject a JWT whose holder cannot show the bound key, which turns a bearer token into a token bound to a key. The RFC deliberately leaves the challenge and response protocol to the application.

today: RFC 7800 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It registers the 'cnf' claim in the IANA JSON Web Token Claims registry and establishes the IANA JWT Confirmation Methods registry with the entries 'jwk', 'jwe', 'kid' and 'jku'.

sections.title: Binding a Token to a Key
sections.content:
RFC 7519 defines the JSON Web Token (JWT), a compact object that carries a set of claims and is integrity protected by its issuer. This RFC adds one more thing a JWT can say: that the party presenting it holds a particular proof-of-possession key. Proof of possession of a key is also described as the presenter being a holder-of-key.

The RFC describes two cases. In the symmetric case (Figure 1), the presenter or the issuer generates a shared secret and passes it to the other party privately. The issuer puts an encrypted copy of that secret into the confirmation claim of the JWT, encrypted with a key known only to the issuer and the recipient, which was established before. The JWT is integrity protected by the issuer and sent to the presenter, who now holds both the secret and the JWT. When the presenter later presents the JWT, it also demonstrates possession of the secret, for example in a challenge and response exchange. The recipient decrypts the key from the confirmation claim and uses it to verify the cryptographically protected messages. The RFC notes that this is conceptually similar to a Kerberos ticket.

In the asymmetric case (Figure 2), the presenter generates a public and private key pair and sends the public key to the issuer, which creates a JWT containing that public key, or an identifier for it, in the confirmation claim, and integrity protects the JWT with a digital signature. The presenter then demonstrates possession of the private key, for example by using it in a Transport Layer Security (TLS) exchange with the recipient or by signing a nonce chosen by the recipient. The recipient checks the signature of the JWT, extracts the public key and verifies the TLS exchange or the nonce signature.

The RFC also notes that the symmetric case is safer when the keys actually used are derived from the exchanged secret with a Key Derivation Function (KDF) rather than used directly.
sections.plainLanguage: A token can now be tied to a key that the person presenting it must hold. There are two ways to do that. With a shared secret, the token carries a scrambled copy of the secret that only the issuer and the receiver can open. With a key pair, the token carries the public half and the presenter signs something with the private half. Either way, copying the token does not let a thief use it.

sections.title: Issuer, Presenter and Recipient
sections.content:
The RFC uses the terms defined in the JSON Web Token, JSON Web Key and JSON Web Encryption specifications, and adds three of its own.

  • The issuer creates the JWT and binds the proof-of-possession key to it.
  • The presenter proves possession of a private key, for asymmetric key cryptography, or a secret key, for symmetric key cryptography, to a recipient.
  • The recipient receives the JWT containing the proof-of-possession key information from the presenter.

The presenter can be identified in several ways, depending on the application. If the JWT contains a 'sub' (subject) claim, the presenter is normally the subject it names; in some applications that identifier is relative to the issuer named by the 'iss' (issuer) claim. If the JWT contains no 'sub' claim, the presenter is normally the issuer. At least one of the 'sub' and 'iss' claims must be present, and some use cases require both. Some applications use an explicit claim such as the 'azp' (authorized party) claim from OpenID Connect. The choice is application specific, as is the means of confirming possession of the key.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties matter. The issuer creates the token and attaches the key to it. The presenter is the party that hands the token over and has to prove it holds the key. The recipient is the party that checks. The token normally names the presenter, either with a subject claim or with the issuer claim.

sections.title: The Confirmation Claim
sections.content:
A JWT declares the key it is bound to by including a 'cnf' (confirmation) claim. The value of that claim is a JSON object, and the members of the object identify the proof-of-possession key. Other members may be defined, because a proof-of-possession key may not be the only means of confirming the authenticity of the token. The RFC compares this to the SubjectConfirmation element in SAML 2.0, where several confirmation methods can be listed, including proof-of-possession key information.

Which members a JWT must contain to be considered valid depends on the context and is outside the scope of this specification. Applications will require implementations to understand particular members in particular ways, and in the absence of such requirements, confirmation members that are not understood must be ignored.

The 'cnf' claim value must represent only a single proof-of-possession key, so at most one of the 'jwk', 'jwe' and 'jku' confirmation values defined by the RFC may be present. An application that needs several proof-of-possession keys in the same JWT can use other claim names, with the same syntax and semantics, defined by the application or by another specification and registered in the IANA JSON Web Token Claims registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The 'cnf' claim is a small object inside the token whose members point at the key. It holds one key only, so a token that needs several keys uses separate claims. Members the software does not understand are ignored rather than treated as errors.

sections.title: Carrying the Key in the Token
sections.content:
When the key held by the presenter is an asymmetric private key, the 'jwk' member of the confirmation claim holds a JSON Web Key (RFC 7517) representing the matching public key. The JWK must contain the required members for its key type and may contain others, including 'kid' (Key ID). The RFC's example uses an elliptic curve key on curve P-256.

The 'jwk' member may also carry a symmetric key, provided the JWT is encrypted so the key is not revealed to unintended parties. If the JWT is not encrypted, a symmetric key must be encrypted as described below.

When the key held by the presenter is a symmetric key, the 'jwe' member holds an encrypted JSON Web Key, encrypted to a key known to the recipient using the JWE Compact Serialization and containing the symmetric key. The rules for encrypting a JWK are in Section 7 of RFC 7517. The UTF-8 encoding of the JWK is used as the JWE Plaintext, and the RFC's example JWE Header names the RSA-OAEP algorithm and the A128CBC-HS256 encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: A public key is put straight into the token in the 'jwk' member, because a public key needs no protection. A shared secret is not, because anyone who can read the token would then have it. The 'jwe' member carries the secret encrypted for the recipient, so only the recipient can open it.

sections.title: Naming a Key Instead of Sending It
sections.content:
The proof-of-possession key can also be identified by a key ID instead of being sent, provided the recipient is able to obtain the identified key using that ID. The issuer then puts a JSON object with a 'kid' member in the confirmation claim. The content of the 'kid' value is application specific; some applications may use a JWK Thumbprint, as defined in RFC 7638.

The key can also be passed by reference rather than by value, using the 'jku' member. Its value is a URI that refers to a resource holding a set of JSON-encoded public keys represented as a JWK Set, one of which is the proof-of-possession key. If the referenced JWK Set document contains multiple keys, a 'kid' member must also be included, and the referenced key's JWK must carry the same 'kid' value.

The protocol used to acquire the resource must provide integrity protection. An HTTP GET request to retrieve the JWK Set must use TLS, and the identity of the server must be validated as described in Section 6 of RFC 6125.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of putting the key in the token, the token can name it. With 'kid' the recipient already knows how to find the key. With 'jku' the token points at a web address where the recipient fetches the keys, and the RFC requires that fetch to use TLS with the server identity checked.

sections.title: What the RFC Leaves to the Application
sections.content:
Proof of possession is typically demonstrated by having the presenter sign a value determined by the recipient, a value sometimes called a nonce or a challenge. The means of communicating the nonce, and the nature of its contents, are intentionally not described in this specification, because different protocols communicate this information in different ways. The means of communicating the signed nonce is also not specified, as that is protocol specific too.

Another way of proving possession of a symmetric key is to encrypt the key to the recipient. How the recipient obtains the key for that purpose is likewise protocol specific.

The specification therefore defines how the key is communicated in the token, and leaves the exchange that proves possession to the protocol that uses it. The RFC points to the OAuth 2.0 Proof-of-Possession security architecture work for examples of the mechanisms defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC deliberately stops short of the actual challenge and response. It says how to put the key in the token, and leaves the exchange that proves the holder has it to whatever protocol is using the token.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of Bound Tokens
sections.content:
All of the security considerations that apply to the JWT itself also apply here, and proof of possession adds its own. Possessing a key is only valuable if it is kept secret, so appropriate means must be used to keep private key and symmetric key values from unintended parties. Applications using proof of possession should also use audience restriction, which gives different protections: proof of possession lets a recipient reject messages from unauthorized senders, while audience restriction lets it reject messages meant for someone else.

A recipient might not understand the 'cnf' claim. Applications that require the proof-of-possession keys communicated with it to be understood and processed must ensure that the parts of the specification they use are implemented.

Proof of possession via encrypted symmetric secrets is subject to replay attacks. This can be avoided when a signed nonce or challenge is used, because the recipient can use a distinct value for each interaction. Replay can also be avoided if a sub-key is derived from a shared secret specific to that instance of the proof-of-possession demonstration.

As with any information in a JWT, data origin authentication and integrity protection are needed, by a keyed message digest or a digital signature. Integrity protection prevents an adversary from changing elements in the payload, and special care is needed when carrying symmetric keys inside the JWT, because those need confidentiality protection as well as integrity protection.

For privacy, a proof-of-possession key can act as a correlation handle if the same key is used with several parties, so different keys are recommended when interacting with different parties.
sections.plainLanguage: The key bound to the token is only useful if it stays secret, so the token itself still needs the usual protection against changes and impersonation. A replayed token is a real risk with the shared-secret method, and the RFC suggests using a fresh value for each exchange. For privacy, use a different key with each party, because reusing one lets the parties be linked to each other.
